facts.statement: Bagaraatan is a Mongolian theropod dinosaur genus named for its small size and meaning 'small carnivorous animal' in Mongolian.
facts.quote: Bagaraatan (/'ba-ɣa-raa-tan/ meaning 'small' baɣa + 'carnivorous animal, beast of prey' araatan in Mongolian) is a genus of theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous period of what is now the Nemegt Formation of Mongolia.

facts.statement: Bagaraatan was likely a small predator reaching approximately 3 to 4 meters in length.
facts.quote: It may have been a small predatory dinosaur measuring around 3 to 4 m in length.

facts.statement: The species Bagaraatan ostromi was first described by Halszka Osmólska in 1996.
facts.quote: The type species, B. ostromi, was described by Halszka Osmólska in 1996.

facts.statement: The holotype skeleton of Bagaraatan resembles juvenile Tyrannosaurus and Tarbosaurus, suggesting it was one of the smallest known tyrannosaurids.
facts.quote: Similarities between the material and young specimens of Tyrannosaurus and Tarbosaurus indicate that the holotype represents a juvenile tyrannosaurid, one of the smallest currently known.

facts.statement: Later analysis revealed that the original material attributed to Bagaraatan was a mix of bones from two different dinosaurs, including hand bones and a femur from a caenagnathid.
facts.quote: The material that warranted this conclusion was later found to be a chimaera of two non-avian dinosaurs, with some of the post-crania (hand bones, left femur, tibiotarsus, and rib) being referred to an indeterminate caenagnathid, possibly Elmisaurus.

facts.statement: A 2024 study confirmed that the initial material assigned to Bagaraatan was a chimaera of different dinosaur species.
facts.quote: In their 2024 reassessment of Bagaraatan, Słowiak, Brusatte & Szczygielski determined that the initial material referred to Bagaraatan is chimaeric.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the holotype material of Bagaraatan likely belongs to the Tyrannosauridae family or a closely related group.
facts.quote: They suggested that the material recognized as the holotype can more confidently be identified as a member of the Tyrannosauridae or a closely related tyrannosauroid.

facts.statement: Scientists caution that the exact evolutionary position of Bagaraatan remains uncertain because juvenile tyrannosaurids often appear more primitive in phylogenetic trees.
facts.quote: However, they caution that its exact phylogenetic position remains uncertain since juvenile specimens tend to be recovered in more basal positions than adults of the same species.

facts.statement: Bagaraatan lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)
